A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-classification experiments, dataset analyses, distribution-shift tests, scalability measurements, and inductive and missingness-mask ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds RelBench performance and runtime measurements, reverse-distribution-shift results, and embedding and additional-baseline experiments.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure still concatenates missingness indicators with filled features and processes them through a GNN. RDLmim applies this same augmentation to the existing RDL pipeline, explicitly retaining its other components. No new missing-feature algorithm, learning objective, or inference procedure is specified.

E1.justification: v2 adds five tasks from REL-EVENT, REL-TRIAL, REL-ARXIV, and REL-F1, extending evaluation to large temporal relational graphs with naturally occurring missingness and to node regression. Table 54 also adds the reverse shift from U-MCAR training to MNAR testing. The original datasets and test scenarios remain.

E2.justification: The original comparator suite is retained. v2 adds evaluated comparisons against RDL on RelBench, MICE+GNN on four datasets, MLP+MIM and XGBoost on three datasets, and AE-GNN in the AIR representation experiment. These introduce substantial new comparison families.

E3.justification: New RelBench experiments use MAE or ROC-AUC, matched ten-epoch budgets without early stopping, validation-selected checkpoints, neighbor sampling, and a nearly complete control dataset. Additional protocols compare raw AIR features with 256-dimensional autoencoder embeddings and reverse the original missingness-shift direction. These are added protocols, not established reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds reverse-shift robustness testing in Table 54, an empirical test of embedding redundancy in Appendix K, and non-graph comparisons testing the contribution of graph structure in Appendix L. The earlier scalability, inductive, and mask-augmentation analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The original five-run reporting remains. New RelBench experiments explicitly report means and standard deviations across three seeds, identified as 0, 1, and 2. Table 2 replaces individual KS-test p-values with their overall range, reducing statistical detail. Neither change establishes an increase in runs for existing experiments.

E6.justification: RelBench, reverse-shift, embedding, and additional-baseline results substantially expand the evidence. Some existing AIR values also change: FP under S-MCAR at missingness 0.99 changes from 0.350 in v1 Table 28 to 0.450 in v2 Table 29. Most original results remain identical. The new reverse-shift results include substantial GCNmf advantages over GNNmim on ELECTRIC.

T1.justification: The main definitions, theorems, and proofs are retained. New Remark A.1 identifies conditions making steps of the information-loss bound tight, including injective deterministic labels, independent feature entries, and identical marginals. This adds mathematical reasoning without changing the bound itself.

C1.justification: The central claims about inadequate benchmarks, realistic missingness protocols, and a competitive simple baseline remain. The abstract and fourth contribution shift emphasis from introducing GNNmim to adapting MIM, while explicitly extending competitiveness to naturally occurring missingness. The novelty claim is narrowed to graph node-level tasks under arbitrary missingness and distribution shifts.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops explanations of embedding redundancy, the contribution of message passing relative to non-graph models, and applicability under unknown natural missingness. It adds qualifications about bound tightness and explicit task limitations. The earlier proposed future direction of graph-structure-dependent MNAR mechanisms is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link beyond the existing supplementary-material statement. Appendix E.1 documents RelBench architecture, optimizer, learning rate, batching, sampling, text preprocessing, hardware, checkpoint selection, and runtime measurement. Table 5 newly documents FP and PCFI backbone selections; this disclosure alone does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges earlier missingness-indicator applications through Cao et al. and Cini et al., narrowing its novelty positioning. It also substantially expands discussion and citations concerning learned embeddings, GraphLand, OGB, GraphBench, relational learning, and classical and non-graph baselines. These extend the research positioning beyond bibliographic corrections.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative and much of the original prose remain. Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, introduction, results discussion, and conclusion; terminology changes include zero-padding to zero-filling. v2 adds Q4, an explicit limitations paragraph, and appendix sections without broadly reorganizing the existing argument.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with resized and redrawn plots, revised legends, and a different heatmap palette. Dataset statistics are consolidated, Table 2 is transposed, and the backbone table is expanded. New RelBench, benchmark-audit, and reverse-shift tables and Figures 9–11 substantially extend the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1's practical relevance relied on artificially imposed missingness and synthetic scaling tests. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with naturally missing relational classification and regression tasks, matched comparisons, and runtime measurements in Table 3. The reverse-shift, embedding, and non-graph analyses further test important robustness and benchmarking assumptions. These gains, supported by better reproducibility information and narrower novelty positioning, outweigh reduced p-value detail and limited discussion of unfavorable reverse-shift results.
